title: Teams That Spin Without Making Critical Priorities and Decisions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article diagnoses a specific team dysfunction: leaders who prize consensus so highly that they let discussions circle endlessly without ever landing on a decision. It explains that this pattern often stems from a leader's reluctance to exercise authority, even when consensus genuinely cannot be reached on a critical issue. The author is careful to affirm the value of building consensus where possible, but argues that leaders must recognize the moment when further discussion has stopped being productive and step in to make the call. The piece recommends setting explicit timelines for discussion so that the team knows a decision is coming, preventing the frustration and eroded candor that come from open-ended deliberation.
points: The essay pinpoints a specific leadership failure — over-attachment to consensus — as the mechanism that causes team 'spinning,' rather than blaming the team itself.
It offers a concrete fix: setting a reasonable timeline for discussion so the team knows when the leader will step in and decide.
It notes a secondary cost of unresolved spinning that's easy to miss: candor itself deteriorates when no end to debate is in sight.
The piece draws a clear boundary between building consensus (good, worth the effort) and clinging to consensus past its usefulness (destructive).
quotes: Leaders who prefer to operate as a peer or cling to a commitment to consensus can create quite a problem for an otherwise effective group.
Good leaders don’t use their decision-making rights until they need to. They prefer to allow the team to reach consensus on even the weightiest issues.
Teams spin anytime they continue to discuss an issue without a deadline for resolution. They rehash and retrace arguments over and over.
Frustration builds and team members tire of the never-ending discussion loop. Candor suffers when no end seems in sight. What a mess.
The best leaders set a reasonable timeline for the team to fully explore any issue and to reach agreement as to what to do about it.
